title: First Bad Version
prompt: You are a product manager tasked with finding which version of a product broke. You have `n` versions labeled `1` to `n`, and you know that once a version is bad, every version after it is also bad. You are given the first bad version, `bad`, as an integer (representing what an `is_bad_version(version)` API would tell you internally). Implement `first_bad_version(n, bad)`, which should behave as if it only had access to a boolean `is_bad_version` check (treat `bad` as data the checker uses internally, not something to read directly), and return the first bad version while calling that check as few times as possible.

examples.explanation: Versions 1-3 are good, versions 4-5 are bad, so the first bad version is 4.
When only the very last version is bad, the search must narrow all the way to the upper boundary.

constraints: The bad version, once it exists, makes every later version bad too
hints: Calling is_bad_version on every version from 1 to n finds the answer in O(n) calls, but the good/bad split is monotonic, which suggests something faster.
Because all versions before the first bad one are good and all versions from it onward are bad, this is a search over a boolean array with a single false-to-true transition.
Binary search for that transition point: if mid is bad, the answer is mid or earlier; if mid is good, the answer is strictly later.

solution.approach: The versions form a monotonic sequence of good...good, bad...bad, so binary search for the boundary. Wrap the given `bad` threshold in a simple `is_bad_version(version)` check (version >= bad), exactly mirroring the real API. At each step check mid: if it's bad, the first bad version is mid or something smaller, so move high to mid; if it's good, the first bad version must be later, so move low to mid + 1. When low equals high, that index is the first bad version, found in O(log n) calls instead of O(n).
